title: Rates of change: change per unit of input
explanation:
Before any calculus, a rate is just a ratio of two changes: how far the output moved divided by how far the input moved. If a bath loses 30 L while 10 minutes pass, it drains at 3 L *per minute*. The units tell the story (output units per input unit), so a rate in L/min can never be confused with an amount in L.

On a graph, that ratio is the slope of the **secant line** through two points $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$: $\frac{\Delta f}{\Delta x}=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. OpenStax uses exactly this slope to estimate "the rate at which one variable changes in relation to another variable" [1], and 3Blue1Brown reads a distance-time graph the same way: slope is rise over run for each interval [2].

The sign carries meaning. A positive average rate means the output rose over the interval; a negative one means it fell. An average also hides detail: two journeys with the same start and end values have the same average rate, however differently they moved in between.
keyIdeas: Average rate = change in output ÷ change in input.
A rate's units are output units per input unit.
On a graph the average rate is the slope of the secant line through two points.
Positive rate: the output rose. Negative rate: it fell.

workedExample.problem: A tank holds $60$ L at $t=1$ min and $18$ L at $t=7$ min. Find its average rate of change of volume.
steps: Name the changes: $\Delta V = 18-60 = -42$ L and $\Delta t = 7-1 = 6$ min.
Predict the sign: the volume went down, so the rate must be negative.
workedExample.answer: $-7$ L/min (on average the tank loses 7 L each minute)

pitfalls: Subtracting in mismatched order, e.g. $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{a-b}$, which flips the sign.
Dropping units: without 'per' units you cannot tell whether you divided the right way round.
Treating an average rate as the rate at every moment of the interval.
